queries.note: 11 resolved in one call; 4 further in the first (rate-limited) retry sequence.
Text returned for most; EMPTY for PMC5529892, PMC8174970, PMC7056001, PMC7974047 (abstract only) and PMC4333991. Full texts of the case reports were grepped for paraphysis/origin statements.

failures: Wiley Scholar Gateway free-tier quota exhausted (resets 2026-11-01): no Wiley confirmation possible in this label.
PubMed MCP returned RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED twice (convert_article_ids, get_article_metadata/search); retried after a short pause, no data lost.

get_full_text_article returned empty full text for PMC5529892 (Mukherjee 2017), PMC8174970 and PMC7056001 (Kier letters), PMC7974047 (Armao 2000, abstract only) and PMC4333991; the Mukherjee and Armao paraphysis sentences therefore rest on WebSearch quotations only (access=web_snippet).

Armao 2000 sentence on the human paraphysis (7th week, degeneration ~3.5 months) appeared inside two WebSearch summaries but was not reproduced by a verbatim-phrase search; verify against the AJNR page before citing.

The 'Haymaker and Yenermen 1955' series named in a WebSearch summary could not be confirmed; PubMed gives Yenermen, Bowerman & Haymaker 1958 (Acta Neuroveg 17:211-277). Fulton & Bailey 1929 and Streeter 1912 are not in PubMed (web items, bibliographic_verified=false).
J Liaquat Univ Med Health Sci Vol 5 No 1 case report (PDF v5n1cr01) contains the phrase 'vestigial structure of paraphysis' per WebSearch, but its title/authors could not be retrieved; not recorded.

Not recorded because no bibliographic identity could be obtained or content was imaging/clinical only: J Neurosci Rural Pract commentary on Kurwale 2013, Int J Gen Med 2018 (S169018, lookup AMBIGUOUS), Cent Eur Neurosurg 2004;65:108, Neurocirugia 'quiste neuroepitelial coloide rolandico', Spanish Medigraphic case reports, StatPearls NBK470314, Radiopaedia 'Paraphysis elements', thefetus.net case 493, Medscape and Neurosurgical Atlas pages (leads only).

No human fetal atlas, embryology textbook passage or modern study assigning the human paraphysis to a Carnegie stage was found with the available channels; human paraphysis development remains documented only by Kappers 1955 (already held), Warren 1917, Bailey 1916 and second-hand statements (Armao 2000, 1954 conference).
WebSearch output is AI-written: all web_snippet excerpts are sentences quoted inside such summaries and must not be cited as direct quotations of the original papers.

records.title: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle: imaging-pathologic correlation.
records.authors: Armao D, Castillo M, Chen H, Kwock L
records.query: colloid cyst third ventricle "paraphysis" embryologic origin review ... 2015..2025 (WebSearch, extended)
records.excerpt: The human paraphysis develops as a pouchlike evagination of the diencephalic roof dorsal to the interventricular foramen in the 7th week of life. Paraphyseal rudiments normally disappear by total degeneration at approximately 3.5 months of age. Colloid cysts of the third ventricle may arise from detached, nondegenerating embryonic vesicular recesses.
records.note: Gives a timetable for the human paraphysis (outgrowth week 7, total degeneration ~3.5 months) and a detached-vesicle origin for colloid cysts; NB the quoted text describes a DIENCEPHALIC-roof origin whereas the classical papers place the paraphysis on the telencephalic roof rostral to the velum transversum. PubMed abstract itself only says etiology is debated and discusses cholesterol/MRI correlation.
records.as_cited_in: Quoted inside two WebSearch AI summaries of the full text (AJNR 21:1470); the PMC fetch returned only the abstract and a verbatim-phrase re-search did not reproduce the sentence, so check against the AJNR page before citing

records.title: Huge familial colloid cyst of the third ventricle: An extraordinary presentation.
records.authors: Niknejad HR, Samii A, Shen SH, Samii M
records.query: Surgical Neurology International colloid cyst third ventricle pathogenesis paraphysis review (WebSearch) -> PMC full text
records.excerpt: More than a century ago Sjovall presumed the cysts originated out of the paraphysis cerebri, an evanescent vestigial embryonic structure.[] This theory held state until the advent of the term “neuroepithelial cyst” in 1929 by Fulton and Bailey. They discussed the presence of cilia and certain cyst contents in their specimens along with the variability in the location of the cysts, holding both a pathological and an anatomical argument against a paraphyseal origin.
records.note: Open-access SNI paper whose Discussion ("The origin of colloid cysts") gives a compact historiography: Sjovall (paraphysis) -> Fulton & Bailey 1929 (neuroepithelial cyst, argued against paraphyseal origin) -> Kappers 1955 (ectopic cyst from displaced paraphyseal anlagen of ependymal origin) -> Coxe & Luse 1964 (ependymal, EM) -> Shuangshoti (paraphysis classified as extraventricular choroid plexus) -> Tsuchida / Ho & Garcia (endodermal, respiratory-type); also Prop1 analogy with Rathke cysts for familial cases. Secondary source: the primary dates/attributions are the authors' and should be checked in the originals.

records.title: Intraventricular sizeable colloid cyst with atypical radiological features: A case report and evidence-based review.
records.authors: Mansour MA, Khalil DF, Hamdi A, Bayoumi M, El-Salamoni MA, Elsoulia A, Lasheen AA, Kamel AE, Nawara M, Ayad AA
records.query: colloid cyst AND (histogenesis OR endodermal OR neuroepithelial OR paraphysis OR embryological OR embryogenesis) -> PMC full text
records.excerpt: Thus far, neuropathologists still debate the true origin of colloid cysts. Colloid cysts were thought to originate from the neuroectodermal elements of the paraphysis cerebri [,]. However, recent immunohistochemistry studies have challenged the notion of the neuroepithelial origin of colloid cysts by the presence of several different cell types lining the cyst capsule, including ciliated and nonciliated, goblet, basal, and squamous cells, suggesting an endodermal rather than ectodermal origin of these colloid cysts.
records.note: Open-access case + review that illustrates the modern textbook position: paraphysis (neuroectodermal) origin described as superseded by endodermal-migration models on immunohistochemical grounds.

records.title: Colloid Cyst Presenting With Severe Headache and Bilateral Leg Weakness: Case Report and Review.
records.authors: Nadeem A, Espinosa J, Lucerna A
records.query: colloid cyst paraphysis ... (WebSearch, cureus.com / PMC) -> PMC full text
records.excerpt: The origin of a colloid cyst has been proposed to be a possible human remnant of sensory cells in lower vertebrates. The theory holds that these cells, which are epithelial in origin, slowly grow in size as they accumulate secretory debris []. Another theory is the development of pouch-like evagination of the diencephalic roof during embryologic development [].
records.note: Cureus case + review; origin paragraph alludes to remnant of cells of lower vertebrates and to a pouch-like evagination of the diencephalic roof (the paraphysis is NOT named, and "sensory cells" does not match the usual description of the paraphysis as a secretory ependymal structure - treat as imprecise).

records.excerpt: Congenital origin of these cysts is accepted universally; however, cell of origin is highly debated.[] Initial reports suggested their neuroepithelial origin as the derivatives of paraphysis or ventricular ependyma and these were further supported later by other studies.[] However, Mackenzie[] in 1991 suggested the endodermal derivation of these cysts on the basis of ultrastructural features which was supported by other authors.[] Until recently endodermal derivation of these cysts enjoyed the favor when Nagaraju.,[] in 2010 reignited the debate by claiming colloid cysts as paraphysis remnants in human.
records.note: Full-text discussion: summarises neuroepithelial (paraphysis/ependyma) vs endodermal origin, the association of colloid cysts with midline malformations (callosal agenesis, encephaloceles, cavum veli interpositi) and Cheng et al.'s "anterior neuropore corridor defects" model in which a vacuolated paraphysis becomes the cyst.

records.excerpt: The origin of "colloid" cysts is from neuroepithelium; these cysts arise from both ependyma and choroid plexus. Those cysts arising in or near the floor of the third ventricle may originate in stomodeal epithelium, but a distinction cannot be made from neuroepithelial cysts by presently available methods.
records.note: States the Shuangshoti/Netsky position (neuroepithelial, from ependyma and choroid plexus) while conceding a possible stomodeal origin for cysts near the third-ventricle floor.

records.authors: Ciric I, Zivin I

records.excerpt: In view of their origin from the neuroepithelium in the diencephalic roof, whether by a process of invagination into the third ventricle or by evagination into the velum interpositum, the so-called colloid cysts are more appropriately termed neuroepithelial cysts.
records.note: Two cysts between the fornices/septal leaves; discusses pathogenesis "in light of the developmental anatomy" and proposes origin from diencephalic-roof neuroepithelium (invagination into the third ventricle or evagination into the velum interpositum).
